description: Around 1601, Shakespeare wrote Hamlet, a prince who hesitates after his father's murder. Between revenge, feigned madness, and the question “To be or not to be,” the modern hero of conscience is born.

hero.hook: A ghost, a prince who cannot decide, and the most famous question in all of theater.

blocks.text: Around **1601**, **William Shakespeare** wrote **[[Hamlet, Prince of Denmark]]**. It is more than a revenge tragedy: it is the portrait of a modern mind, torn between action and doubt. The soliloquy “**To be or not to be**” has become the great existential question of Western theater.

Ghosts, feigned madness, a final duel: the play mixes the supernatural with psychology long before psychology had a name. Hamlet is nothing like the impulsive heroes of classical drama, who strike at once. He thinks too much to act fast, and that is exactly what makes him immortal. Shakespeare invents a character who doubts everything, himself included.

Shakespeare wrote at the high point of English theater, under **Elizabeth I**. The plays went up at the **Globe Theatre**, a round wooden building open to the sky, where rich and poor stood or sat side by side according to what they could pay. Every actor was a man: the female parts went to teenage boys, as the law of the day required.

blocks.caption: William Shakespeare, author of the most discussed tragedy in the world

blocks.text: The part of Ophelia was first played by a boy whose voice had not yet broken, following the custom of the time.

blocks.caption: The Globe Theatre: the Elizabethan stage where Hamlet won its audience

blocks.text: Shakespeare was after the truth of the heart rather than flat realism. Hamlet comes home from his studies at **[[Wittenberg]]**, the German university town that was the cradle of the **Protestant Reformation**. Inside the play, Shakespeare stages another play, “The Mousetrap,” to trap **Claudius** and test the king's guilt. Theater becomes a mirror of the world and a tool for finding the truth.

sections.title: The Elizabethan stage: a theater of the world

blocks.text: The king of Denmark is murdered by his brother **Claudius**, who marries Queen **Gertrude** and takes the throne. The dead king's ghost reveals the crime to **Hamlet**. The duty looks clear: avenge the father. But Hamlet doubts. Is this specter really his father, or a lying demon? And is revenge just in the eyes of Christian morality?

Torn between **[[lex talionis]]**, the old law of an eye for an eye, and a Christian conscience that forbids killing, he feigns madness so he can investigate without raising suspicion. The plan fails: he breaks the heart of **Ophelia**, daughter of the counselor **Polonius**, and then kills Polonius by mistake, stabbing him through a curtain. The machinery grinds on to the final slaughter at the Danish court, where almost every main character dies.

sections.title: The spiral of revenge and the weight of hesitation

blocks.text: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” The play breathes moral decay. Hamlet's language is soaked in images of sickness, rot, and corpses. **[[Melancholy in the 16th century]]** leaves him brilliant but paralyzed: in Shakespeare's day it counted as a medical humor, tied to creativity but also to inaction.

blocks.caption: Hamlet and Yorick's skull: death mocks every ambition

blocks.attribution: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act III, Scene 1
blocks.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question.

The famous soliloquy questions existence itself: is it better to endure the pain of living, or to die and escape it? To act is to dirty yourself in a corrupt world. Not to act is to let evil win. Hamlet becomes the first modern hero, unable to reconcile thought with deed. **[[Elizabethan revenge and honor]]** explains part of his paralysis: a man of honor was expected to avenge an insult to his family, yet that duty pulled against both the law and Christian morality.

sections.title: Melancholy and the rot of Denmark

blocks.text: For four centuries Hamlet has been reinterpreted without end. The **Romantics** of the 19th century saw in him the tormented artist. **Freud** read the play through the **[[Oedipus complex]]**. It speaks about losing a parent, about the darkness of the world, and about the painful crossing into adulthood.

Its influence runs well past the stage: film, opera, comics, popular psychology. Shakespeare turned a medieval ghost story into a metaphysical inquiry into human consciousness. Hamlet remains the tragedy of indecision, where thinking is already a form of suffering.
**Hamlet** shows that a hero can be immortal not because he acts fast, but because he doubts deeply. Shakespeare invents modern theater here: to think is already to suffer.
